The block below is given. It follows the chapter’s steps to compute the PMI of every bigram and saves the result as pmi, with one row per bigram. Run it and look at the table.



View code
bigrams = (
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .with_columns(
        next_token = c.lemma.shift(-1).over([c.doc_id, c.sid])
    )
    .filter(c.next_token.is_not_null())
    .with_columns(
        bigram = c.lemma + " " + c.next_token
    )
)

word_counts = (
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(word_count = pl.len())
)

total_words = word_counts.select(c.word_count.sum()).item()
total_bigrams = bigrams.height

pmi = (
    bigrams
    .group_by(c.bigram, c.lemma, c.next_token)
    .agg(bigram_count = pl.len())
    .join(
        word_counts.rename({"lemma": "w1", "word_count": "w1_count"}),
        left_on=c.lemma,
        right_on=c.w1
    )
    .join(
        word_counts.rename({"lemma": "w2", "word_count": "w2_count"}),
        left_on=c.next_token,
        right_on=c.w2
    )
    .with_columns(
        p_bigram = c.bigram_count / total_bigrams,
        p_w1 = c.w1_count / total_words,
        p_w2 = c.w2_count / total_words
    )
    .with_columns(
        pmi = (c.p_bigram / (c.p_w1 * c.p_w2)).log()
    )
    .select(c.bigram, c.bigram_count, c.pmi)
)

Setup
Run all of the following before starting the notebook.


View code
! wget -q -nc https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/funs.py




View code
import polars as pl
from plotnine import ggplot, aes
from polars import col as c

import funs

ub = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/"




View code
klog = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/keylog.csv.gz")
meta = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/keylog-meta.csv.gz")




Questions
klog is a keystroke log of 823 people typing in English, one row per key press. t0 and t1 give the moment of the press and the release, dur is the hold time in between, and dur_after is the hold time of the next key press. input is the resulting character, null for space and every other key that produces no character, and code is the physical key. meta carries three facts about each of the 823 people behind id: age, native lang, and cefr, a proficiency band for English (A1/A2 weakest, C1/C2 strongest). t0 and t1 are milliseconds elapsed since each person’s recording started, not wall-clock times, so they contain no year, month, or day. Print results unless a question says otherwise.

Using meta, draw a bar plot with .geom_bar() showing how many people fall in each cefr band.



View code
(
    meta
    .ggplot(aes(c.cefr))
    .geom_bar()
    .labs(title="Participants by CEFR Band", x="CEFR Band", y="Count")
)

Using klog, filter to key presses with dur under 300 milliseconds and draw a histogram of dur with .geom_histogram(bins=60).



View code

    klog
    .filter(c.dur < 300)
    .ggplot(aes(c.dur))
    .geom_histogram(bins=60)
    .labs(title="Key Hold Time", x="Hold Time (ms)", y="Count")
)










The block below is given. It sorts klog by person and press time, then adds three columns. press and release turn t0 and t1 into Datetime values by casting the milliseconds to an integer and then to pl.Datetime("ms"). That reads them as a Unix timestamp, so every session’s clock starts at 1970-01-01 00:00:00 instead of a real date; only the clock time matters, and it means time elapsed since recording began. gap is a Duration: the time between the release of the previous key and the press of this one, computed within each person with .over(c.id). The first key of each session has no previous key, so its gap is null. Run the block and look at the new columns.



View code
klog = (
    klog
    .sort(c.id, c.t0)
    .with_columns(
        press = c.t0.cast(pl.Int64).cast(pl.Datetime("ms")),
        release = c.t1.cast(pl.Int64).cast(pl.Datetime("ms"))
    )
    .with_columns(
        gap = c.press - c.release.shift(1).over(c.id)
    )
